title: About this chatbot and what it can do
text:
# About this chatbot and what it can do

This chatbot is a supportive information tool about mental health and emotional wellbeing. It is a demonstration project. It is not a doctor, nurse, psychologist or counsellor, and it cannot confirm a diagnosis, treat or prescribe. It can give a preliminary screening indication from the symptoms a person describes.

What it can do: explain common feelings and conditions in simple language, teach basic coping skills such as slow breathing and grounding, suggest small practical steps, and encourage people to reach out to real people and health services.

What it cannot do: confirm a diagnosis, recommend or name medicines or doses, replace therapy, or handle emergencies. In an emergency, call 112 or go to the nearest hospital emergency unit.

title: Anxiety and worry
text:
# Anxiety and worry

Anxiety is the body's alarm system. A little anxiety is normal, for example before an exam, an interview or a big decision. It can become a problem when worry is frequent, hard to switch off, or gets in the way of sleep, studies, work or relationships.

## Common signs of anxiety
Physical signs: racing or pounding heart, fast breathing, sweating, shaking, tight chest, upset stomach, tense muscles, headaches, feeling dizzy.
Thinking signs: constant "what if" thoughts, expecting the worst, trouble concentrating, mind going blank.
Behaviour signs: avoiding places or tasks, seeking constant reassurance, being irritable, restlessness.

title: Anxiety and worry
text:
aviour signs: avoiding places or tasks, seeking constant reassurance, being irritable, restlessness.

## What can help right now
Slow breathing: breathe in through the nose for 4 seconds, pause for 2, breathe out slowly through the mouth for 6 seconds. Repeat for 3 to 5 minutes. A longer out-breath helps the body calm down.
Grounding with the senses (5-4-3-2-1): name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste.
Write the worry down, then ask: is this a problem I can act on today, or a "what if" I cannot control? For problems, write one small next step. For "what ifs", practise letting the thought pass.
Move your body: a short walk or light stretching burns off stress energy.
Reduce caffeine and energy drinks, which can make anxiety feel worse.

title: Anxiety and worry
text:
ching burns off stress energy.
Reduce caffeine and energy drinks, which can make anxiety feel worse.

## Longer-term habits
Regular sleep and meals, daily movement, limiting constant news and social media, talking to someone you trust, and facing feared situations in small steps instead of avoiding them. Avoidance feels better in the short term but usually makes anxiety stronger over time.

## When to get professional help
If anxiety lasts for several weeks, is stopping you from doing normal things, comes with frequent panic attacks, or you feel hopeless, please speak to a doctor or a mental health professional. Anxiety is common and treatable.

title: Panic attacks
text:
# Panic attacks

A panic attack is a sudden wave of intense fear with strong body sensations such as pounding heart, shortness of breath, chest tightness, trembling, sweating, dizziness, tingling hands, and a feeling that something terrible will happen or that you are losing control. It usually peaks within about 10 minutes and then fades. Although it feels frightening, a panic attack itself is not dangerous.

title: Panic attacks
text:
ut 10 minutes and then fades. Although it feels frightening, a panic attack itself is not dangerous.

## What to do during a panic attack
1. Remind yourself: "This is a panic attack. It will pass. I am safe."
2. Sit down if you can and loosen tight clothing.
3. Breathe slowly: in for 4 seconds, out for 6 seconds. Fast breathing makes the sensations stronger.
4. Ground yourself: press your feet into the floor and name 5 things you can see around you.
5. Do not fight the wave. Let it rise and fall while you keep breathing slowly.

## After a panic attack
Rest, drink water, and be kind to yourself. Try not to avoid the place where it happened, because avoidance can make attacks more likely.

text:

## Important safety note
Chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting or symptoms that are new, severe or do not settle should be checked urgently by a medical professional, because they can also have physical causes. If in doubt, go to the nearest hospital or call 112. If panic attacks keep coming back, speak to a doctor.

title: Low mood and depression
text:
# Low mood and depression

Everyone feels sad sometimes. Depression is different: low mood or loss of interest that lasts most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, and affects daily life.

## Common signs
Feeling sad, empty, hopeless or numb. Losing interest in things you used to enjoy. Tiredness and low energy. Sleeping too much or too little. Eating much more or much less. Difficulty concentrating or deciding. Feeling worthless or guilty. Pulling away from people. In some people, irritability is the main sign.

## Depression is not weakness
Depression is a health condition. It is not laziness, lack of faith, or a character flaw. It is common, and people recover with support.

title: Low mood and depression
text:
is not laziness, lack of faith, or a character flaw. It is common, and people recover with support.

## Small steps that help
Keep a simple daily routine: wake up, wash, eat and sleep at regular times.
Behavioural activation: depression makes you want to do less, and doing less makes mood worse. Each day, plan one small activity that gives either pleasure (a call with a friend, music, a favourite meal) or achievement (washing clothes, a ten-minute walk, one study task). Start very small and notice how you feel afterwards.
Get daylight and gentle movement every day.
Stay in contact with at least one trusted person, even briefly.
Break big tasks into tiny steps and celebrate finishing them.
Avoid alcohol and other drugs, which usually make low mood worse.

title: Low mood and depression
text:

Avoid alcohol and other drugs, which usually make low mood worse.

## When to get help
Please speak to a doctor or mental health professional if low mood lasts two weeks or more, is getting worse, or affects your studies, work or relationships. If you ever have thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, this is urgent: see the crisis and safety information and contact emergency services at once.

title: Stress, study pressure and burnout
text:
# Stress, study pressure and burnout

Stress is the body's reaction to pressure. Short-term stress can help you perform, but long-term stress without rest can lead to exhaustion, anxiety, low mood and illness.

## Signs of too much stress
Headaches, tight shoulders, poor sleep, tiredness, irritability, difficulty concentrating, forgetting things, changes in appetite, feeling overwhelmed, or losing motivation.

title: Stress, study pressure and burnout
text:
ty concentrating, forgetting things, changes in appetite, feeling overwhelmed, or losing motivation.

## Managing exam and study stress
Plan: list everything you need to do, then pick the three most important tasks for today. Break large topics into small sessions.
Study in blocks: for example 25 to 40 minutes of focused study, then a 5 to 10 minute break away from your phone.
Sleep: all-night studying usually reduces memory and performance. Aim for regular sleep, especially before an exam.
Eat and drink regularly, and move your body daily, even a short walk.
Talk to a friend, classmate or family member rather than carrying the pressure alone.
On exam day: prepare your things the night before, breathe slowly while waiting, and if your mind goes blank, pause, breathe, and start with the question you know best.
Remember that one result does not define your worth or your future.

title: Stress, study pressure and burnout
text:

Remember that one result does not define your worth or your future.

## Burnout
Burnout is deep exhaustion from long-term stress, often with cynicism and feeling that nothing you do matters. Rest, reducing workload where possible, asking for support, and setting boundaries are important. If it lasts, speak to a health professional.

title: Sleep problems
text:
# Sleep problems

Sleep and mental health affect each other. Poor sleep can worsen anxiety and low mood, and worry can make it hard to sleep. Occasional bad nights are normal.

## Healthy sleep habits
Go to bed and wake up at about the same time every day, including weekends.
Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and as cool as comfortable.
Avoid phones and screens for 30 to 60 minutes before bed.
Avoid caffeine (coffee, tea, energy drinks) and heavy meals late in the day.
Use the bed only for sleep, not for studying or scrolling.
Get daylight and some physical activity during the day.

title: Sleep problems
text:
ly for sleep, not for studying or scrolling.
Get daylight and some physical activity during the day.

## If you cannot sleep
Do not lie awake watching the clock. If you are awake for about 20 minutes, get up, sit somewhere dim and do something calm (gentle stretching, quiet music, slow breathing) until you feel sleepy, then return to bed.
Write tomorrow's worries and to-do list on paper before bed to get them out of your head.
Try progressive muscle relaxation: tense each muscle group for 5 seconds then relax it, from your feet up to your face.

## When to get help
If sleep problems last for more than a few weeks, affect your daytime functioning, or come with low mood, anxiety or heavy snoring and pauses in breathing, speak to a doctor.

title: Thinking traps and reframing (basic CBT skills)
text:
# Thinking traps and reframing (basic CBT skills)

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is based on the idea that our thoughts, feelings and actions are linked. When we notice unhelpful thinking patterns and gently challenge them, our feelings can ease.

title: Thinking traps and reframing (basic CBT skills)
text:
linked. When we notice unhelpful thinking patterns and gently challenge them, our feelings can ease.

## Common thinking traps
Catastrophising: expecting the worst possible outcome. ("If I fail this test, my life is over.")
All-or-nothing thinking: seeing things as perfect or a total failure.
Mind reading: assuming you know what others think. ("They think I am stupid.")
Overgeneralising: using words like "always" and "never". ("I always mess up.")
Emotional reasoning: believing something is true because it feels true. ("I feel useless, so I am useless.")
Self-blame: taking responsibility for things outside your control.
Discounting the positive: ignoring good things that happened.

title: Thinking traps and reframing (basic CBT skills)
text:
ility for things outside your control.
Discounting the positive: ignoring good things that happened.

## How to reframe a thought (4 steps)
1. Notice and write the thought. Example: "I failed the quiz, so I am a failure."
2. Name the trap. This one is all-or-nothing thinking and overgeneralising.
3. Look at the evidence. What supports the thought? What does not? What would I say to a friend in this situation?
4. Write a more balanced thought. Example: "I did badly on one quiz. It is disappointing, but I can find out what went wrong and improve."

The aim is not forced positive thinking. It is realistic, kinder and more balanced thinking.

title: Thinking traps and reframing (basic CBT skills)
text:

The aim is not forced positive thinking. It is realistic, kinder and more balanced thinking.

## The thought, feeling, action link
Thought: "Nobody wants to talk to me." Feeling: sad and lonely. Action: stay away from people, which confirms the thought. Changing one part, such as sending one friendly message, can start to change the cycle.

title: Relaxation and grounding exercises
text:
# Relaxation and grounding exercises

## Slow breathing (about 3 minutes)
Sit comfortably. Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds. Pause for 2 seconds. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 seconds. Repeat. Place a hand on your belly and feel it rise and fall.

## 5-4-3-2-1 grounding (about 2 minutes)
Name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch or feel, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. This brings attention back to the present moment.

## Progressive muscle relaxation (about 10 minutes)
Starting with your feet, tighten the muscles for 5 seconds, then release for 10 seconds and notice the difference. Move up through legs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders and face. Breathe slowly throughout.

title: Relaxation and grounding exercises
text:
fference. Move up through legs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders and face. Breathe slowly throughout.

## Body check and release
Notice where you hold tension (jaw, shoulders, hands). Drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw and open your hands. Repeat a few times a day.

## A short pause for hard moments
Stop. Take one slow breath. Notice what you are feeling without judging it. Choose one small next step.

These skills work best when practised regularly when you are calm, so they are easier to use when you are stressed.

title: Grief, loss and loneliness
text:
# Grief, loss and loneliness

## Grief
Grief is the natural response to loss, such as the death of someone close, the end of a relationship, losing a job or moving away. There is no right way or time limit to grieve. People may feel sadness, anger, guilt, numbness, tiredness, difficulty sleeping or concentrating, or waves of emotion that come and go.

What can help: talk about the person or the loss with someone who listens; keep simple routines; eat and rest; allow tears and other feelings; take part in cultural, family or faith rituals that bring comfort; and be patient with yourself. Anniversaries and special days can be hard, so plan support for those days.

Seek help if grief feels unbearable, stops you functioning for a long time, or you have thoughts of harming yourself.

title: Grief, loss and loneliness
text:
f feels unbearable, stops you functioning for a long time, or you have thoughts of harming yourself.

## Loneliness
Loneliness is the painful feeling of being disconnected, and it can happen even around people. It can affect mood and health.

Small steps: send one message or call to someone each day; join a group, class, faith community or sports activity; volunteer; spend time with others even in quiet ways, such as studying together; and share honestly with one trusted person. Connection grows slowly, so start small.

title: Self-esteem and anger
text:
# Self-esteem and anger

## Low self-esteem
Low self-esteem means having a persistently negative opinion of yourself. Comparing yourself with others, especially on social media, often makes it worse because people show only their best moments.

Helpful steps: notice your inner critic and answer it the way you would answer a friend; write down three things you did well each day, however small; set small achievable goals; limit comparison; spend time with people who respect you; and practise saying no without guilt.

## Managing anger
Anger is a normal emotion. It becomes a problem when it leads to shouting, violence or damage to relationships.

title: Self-esteem and anger
text:
normal emotion. It becomes a problem when it leads to shouting, violence or damage to relationships.

Early signs: tight jaw or fists, hot face, fast heartbeat.
What to do: pause before reacting; step away from the situation; breathe slowly (in 4, out 6); walk or exercise to release energy; wait until you are calm before speaking; use "I feel... when... because..." statements instead of blame.
Afterwards, think about what the anger was telling you, such as a need for respect, rest or fairness.

If anger leads to hurting others or yourself, or you feel unable to control it, please seek support from a professional. If someone is in immediate danger, call 112.

title: Alcohol, drugs and mental health
text:
# Alcohol, drugs and mental health

Alcohol and other substances can seem to relieve stress or sadness for a short time, but they usually worsen anxiety, low mood and sleep, and can lead to dependence.

## Signs that substance use may be a problem
Using more than planned, craving it, failing to cut down, neglecting studies, work or family, using to cope with feelings, needing more to get the same effect, or feeling unwell when stopping.

## Where to start
Notice when and why you use. Tell one trusted person. Avoid places and situations that trigger use, and replace them with other activities and support. Do not stop suddenly after heavy long-term use of alcohol or some drugs without medical advice, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

title: Alcohol, drugs and mental health
text:
long-term use of alcohol or some drugs without medical advice, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

If someone has taken a large amount of a substance, is unconscious, very drowsy, having trouble breathing, or seems confused or having a seizure, this is an emergency. Call 112 or go to the nearest hospital immediately.

Recovery is possible, and many people get better with support from health professionals, family and community.

title: How to support a friend or family member
text:
# How to support a friend or family member

## Starting the conversation
Choose a private, calm moment. Say what you have noticed with care: "I have noticed you seem down lately. I am here if you want to talk." Ask open questions such as "How have you been feeling?"

## What helps
Listen without interrupting or judging. Say that their feelings are real and that you are glad they told you. Ask what would help. Offer practical help such as sitting with them, helping them book an appointment, or going with them. Keep checking in over time.

## What to avoid
Do not say "just snap out of it", "others have it worse", or "you just need more faith". Do not promise to keep secrets if their safety is at risk. Do not try to handle everything alone.

title: How to support a friend or family member
text:
". Do not promise to keep secrets if their safety is at risk. Do not try to handle everything alone.

## If you are worried about their safety
Ask directly, calmly and kindly: "Are you thinking about hurting yourself or ending your life?" Asking does not put the idea in their head, and it can be a relief. If they say yes, stay with them, remove access to anything they could use to harm themselves where it is safe to do so, and get urgent help: call 112 or take them to the nearest hospital emergency unit. Involve another trusted adult.

Look after yourself too. Supporting someone is tiring, and you also need rest and support.

title: Crisis and safety information
text:
# Crisis and safety information

## If you or someone else is in immediate danger
Call 112 (Nigeria's national emergency number) or go straight to the nearest hospital emergency unit. If you can, tell a trusted person near you and stay with them. Do not stay alone.

## Warning signs that need urgent attention
Talking about wanting to die or to end one's life, talking about hurting oneself, feeling like a burden or having no reason to live, giving away belongings, saying goodbye, sudden calm after deep despair, thoughts of harming other people, or being unable to stay safe.

title: Crisis and safety information
text:
bye, sudden calm after deep despair, thoughts of harming other people, or being unable to stay safe.

## If you are having thoughts of suicide or self-harm
These thoughts are more common than people think, and they can pass, especially with support. You do not have to face them alone. Right now: tell someone you trust how you feel, move away from anything you could use to hurt yourself, and go to or call emergency services. Intense feelings often rise and fall, and getting through the next hour safely matters.

## How this chatbot responds
When a message suggests a person may be at risk, the chatbot will show emergency information and encourage contacting emergency services and a trusted person. It cannot call anyone for you.

title: Myths, stigma and seeking help
text:
# Myths, stigma and seeking help

## Common myths
Myth: Mental illness is a sign of weakness. Fact: It is a health condition that can affect anyone, and seeking help shows strength.
Myth: It is caused only by spiritual problems or a curse. Fact: Many factors are involved, such as biology, stress, life events and relationships. Faith and community can be a real source of comfort and can sit alongside medical care.
Myth: People with mental illness are dangerous. Fact: Most are not violent, and they are more likely to be harmed than to harm others.
Myth: Talking about suicide makes it more likely. Fact: Talking openly and kindly can reduce risk and open the door to help.
Myth: Mental health problems do not get better. Fact: Many people recover or manage well with support and treatment.

title: Myths, stigma and seeking help
text:
lth problems do not get better. Fact: Many people recover or manage well with support and treatment.

## Why people delay seeking help
Fear of being judged, shame, cost, not knowing where to go, or believing they should cope alone. These are understandable, but earlier support usually leads to better outcomes.

## How to take the first step
Talk to someone you trust. Visit a doctor or health centre and describe your symptoms and how long they have lasted. You can take a family member or friend with you. Ask questions and say if you do not understand something.

text:

## What to expect
A professional will listen, ask about your symptoms, sleep, appetite, mood and daily life, and discuss options such as talking therapy, lifestyle support or other treatments. Only a qualified health professional can diagnose a condition or advise on medicines.

title: Where to find help
text:
# Where to find help

This chatbot is a demonstration and is not linked to any hospital or clinic. It does not have verified opening hours, phone numbers or booking details for any service, and it should not invent them.

## What to do for non-emergency help
Visit the nearest hospital, teaching hospital, primary health centre or a licensed doctor, psychologist or counsellor and ask for mental health support. Ask a trusted person to go with you if that helps.

## Emergencies
Call 112 or go to the nearest hospital emergency unit.

If you ask this chatbot for a specific clinic's hours, location or phone number, explain that you do not have verified details and suggest contacting the facility directly.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:
# Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to

Mental health problems show up as changes in feelings, thinking, behaviour and the body. No single symptom proves a condition. What matters is which features appear together, how long they last (usually two weeks or more) and whether they interfere with school, work, family life or self-care. Only a qualified health professional can confirm a diagnosis. The information below is a preliminary screening guide.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:
health professional can confirm a diagnosis. The information below is a preliminary screening guide.

## Low mood and feeling depressed
Features: persistent sadness or emptiness, loss of interest in things once enjoyed, feeling worthless or guilty, crying easily, tiredness, changes in sleep or appetite, poor concentration, and thoughts that life is not worth living. Commonly linked to: depression. Several of these features lasting two weeks or more suggest the person should see a doctor or counsellor.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:
al of these features lasting two weeks or more suggest the person should see a doctor or counsellor.

## Being moody and mood swings
Features: quick changes between irritability, sadness, anger and calm, snapping at people, and difficulty controlling reactions. Mood swings can come from stress, poor sleep, hormones, substance use, or a mood disorder. Commonly linked to: stress and anger problems, depression, or bipolar disorder when swings are extreme, last for days and include periods of very high energy.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:
or bipolar disorder when swings are extreme, last for days and include periods of very high energy.

## Laughing excessively and unusually high mood
Features: laughing or giggling for no clear reason or far more than the situation calls for, feeling unusually happy, excited or powerful, talking very fast, needing little sleep without feeling tired, restlessness and risky spending or behaviour. Commonly linked to: a manic or hypomanic episode (bipolar disorder), the effect of drugs or alcohol, or severe stress. When it lasts several days and the person sleeps very little, a doctor should see them soon.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to

stress. When it lasts several days and the person sleeps very little, a doctor should see them soon.

## Abnormal behaviour
Features: behaving in ways that are strange or out of character, talking to oneself, being unusually suspicious, aggression, wandering, neglecting washing and eating, or speech that does not make sense. Commonly linked to: psychosis (for example schizophrenia), severe depression or mania, substance effects, or a medical illness such as infection or head injury. Sudden abnormal behaviour needs prompt medical assessment.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:

## Seeing or hearing things that others do not
Features: hearing voices, seeing things that are not there, or strong beliefs that others are watching or plotting against the person. Commonly linked to: psychosis. This needs a doctor's assessment soon and is treated as high risk in this chatbot.

## Anxiety and panic
Features: constant worry, feeling on edge, racing heart, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, fear of something terrible happening, and avoiding places or situations. Commonly linked to: generalised anxiety, panic disorder, social anxiety or stress.

title: Symptoms of mental health problems and the conditions they are commonly linked to
text:

## Sleep, appetite and energy changes
Sleeping far too little or too much, losing appetite or overeating, and constant tiredness often appear together with depression, anxiety or mania and are useful clues when combined with other features.

## Withdrawal and poor concentration
Avoiding friends and family, staying alone, stopping usual activities, forgetfulness and difficulty focusing are common early signs that something is wrong, especially when they are new for the person.

## Important note
A list of features is not a diagnosis. Many people have some of these experiences at times. The chatbot only gives a preliminary indication so that the person knows when to seek proper help.

title: Screening levels: when risk is low, moderate or high
text:
# Screening levels: when risk is low, moderate or high

This chatbot uses a simple threshold based on the number of different features of mental health problems that a person has reported during the conversation. The features counted are: low mood, mood swings, excessive laughing or unusually high mood, abnormal behaviour, sleep change, appetite or energy change, withdrawal, anxiety or panic, and poor concentration.

## Low level (one or two features)
The person reports one or two features, usually mild or recent. Suggested response: reassure, explain that many people have such experiences, give simple self-help steps (regular sleep, talking to someone trusted, exercise, relaxation), and advise seeing a counsellor or doctor if the features last two weeks or more or get worse.

title: Screening levels: when risk is low, moderate or high
text:
tion), and advise seeing a counsellor or doctor if the features last two weeks or more or get worse.

## Moderate level (three or four features)
Several features appear together and probably affect daily life. Suggested response: encourage the person to see a doctor, psychologist or counsellor soon, explain which conditions these features are commonly linked to as a preliminary indication only, and ask whether anyone close can support them.

title: Screening levels: when risk is low, moderate or high
text:
commonly linked to as a preliminary indication only, and ask whether anyone close can support them.

## High level (five or more features, or any severe feature)
The person is at risk when five or more features appear together, or when any one severe feature is present: hearing voices or seeing things others do not, strong beliefs that people are watching or plotting against them, not sleeping for several days, being unable to care for themselves, or any thought of suicide, self-harm, or harming others. Suggested response: express care, advise the person to see a doctor or go to the nearest hospital now, call 112 in an emergency, and not stay alone.

title: Screening levels: when risk is low, moderate or high

## Always urgent
Any mention of suicide, self-harm, wanting to die, harming someone else, abuse or immediate danger is treated as high risk no matter how many other features are present.

## Reminder
The screening level is a preliminary indication, not a diagnosis. It is meant to help a person decide when to seek professional care.
